question: The aggressive purchase of land and real estate through the massive inflow of capital from non-EU countries, has intensified in recent years according to news reports and accounts given by residents in many EU Member States. The phenomenon is particularly noticeable in cross-border areas of major economic and national importance.

The European Commission should strengthen transparency mechanisms for tracing the source of the money and the ownership purpose and structure. It should also investigate the corporate structure, especially where there are shell companies facilitating tax evasion or where there are other economic activities involved.

Lastly, in areas of strategic importance, sales should be subject to stricter controls and approval by the competent authorities of each state when national issues arise. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Will it allow for strict controls in Member States, especially in cross-border areas?
Will it check the type of investment and the source of the money?
Will it check the feasibility of setting up a company?
answer: There is no dedicated horizontal EU-level framework governing the acquisition of real estate. General oversight requirements of real estate acquisitions, including checks on the source of the capital, are therefore largely within the remit of national laws.

When adopting such laws, Member States must respect the EU fundamental freedoms, including the freedom of establishment (1) or under the free movement of capital (2), as well as the provisions of applicable sectorial legislation.

Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1386 (3), which sets out the framework for the screening of foreign direct investment ‘FDI’ applicable as of July 2028, corporate transactions, including in the form of asset deals, will be subject to screening when they raise concerns about potential risks to security or public order.

This includes, inter alia, transactions with potential risks on the land and property necessary for operations of a critical entity or critical infrastructure, farmland exceeding 10 000 ha, military facilities and other sensitive public facilities in the immediate geographical proximity of an EU target.

Furthermore, the revised EU anti-money laundering framework will significantly enhance transparency of real estate ownership. Article 18 of Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (4) establishes a single access point for real estate information in each Member State.

Article 67 of Regulation 2024/1624 (5) requires non-EU legal entities and legal arrangements acquiring EU real estate to submit beneficial ownership information to the central register of the Member State where real estate was acquired. The same requirement applies to non-EU legal entities and legal arrangements that own real estate in the Union that they have acquired after 1 January 2014.

Pursuant to Article 49 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Pursuant to Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. OJ L, 2026/1386, 26.6.2026. OJ L, 2024/1640, 19.6.2024. OJ L, 2024/1624, 19.6.2024.
